_note: Independent worked examples for the wind triangle and a runway's wind components, from the FAA's handbook and knowledge-test supplement (fetched from faa.gov on 2026-11-21), never from the code. Shape and checks as reference/atmosphere.json says.

cases.name: The wind triangle: TC 090, TAS 120, wind 045 at 40: WCA 14 left, TH 076, GS 88
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, 2023), ch. 16, pp. 16-14 to 16-15, Figures 16-20 to 16-23: "The distance flown in 1 hour (GS) is measured as the numbers of units on the TC line (88 NMPH or 88 knots) ... read the TH directly in degrees (076°) ... the WCA is 14° and the wind is from the left; therefore, subtract 14° from TC of 090°, making the TH 076°."
cases.method: The handbook draws the triangle and measures it to the knot and degree; the engine solves it by trigonometry (13.6° left, 76.4°, 88.3 kt), so within 1.

cases.name: Chickasha to Guthrie: TC 031, TAS 115, wind 360 at 10: WCA 3 left, TH 028, GS 106
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, 2023), ch. 16, pp. 16-18 to 16-20, Figure 16-26 (pilot's planning sheet): "Using a wind of 360° at 10 knots, it is determined the WCA is 3° left. This is subtracted from the TC making the TH 28° ... The GS is determined to be 106 knots."
cases.method: A flight computer's whole degrees and knots; the engine's 2.6° left, 28.4° and 106.3 kt are within 1.

cases.name: 120 kt eastward with the air moving eastward at 20 kt: GS 140
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, 2023), ch. 16, p. 16-9, Figure 16-13: "If the mass of air is moving eastward at 20 knots ... the progress of the aircraft over the ground is 120 plus 20 or a GS of 140 knots." Air moving eastward is a wind from 270.

cases.name: 120 kt eastward with the air moving westward at 20 kt: GS 100
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, 2023), ch. 16, p. 16-9, Figure 16-13: "if the mass of air is moving westward at 20 knots, the airspeed of the aircraft remains the same, but GS becomes 120 minus 20 or 100 knots."

cases.name: Sample Problem 10: runway 17, wind 140 at 25: headwind 22, crosswind 13 from the left
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, 2023), ch. 11, p. 11-26, Sample Problem 10 (crosswind component chart): "runway 17 means a direction of 170°; from that subtract the wind direction of 140°. This gives a 30° angular difference ... The headwind component is 22 knots and the crosswind component is 13 knots."
cases.method: Read off the chart to the knot; the engine's 21.7 and 12.5 kt are within 1. The engine signs a crosswind from the left negative; a wind of 140 on a heading of 170 is from the left.

cases.name: Figure 36's example: 40 kt at 30 degrees: headwind 35, crosswind 20
cases.source: FAA-CT-8080-2H (Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement for Sport, Recreational, Remote and Private Pilot, 2018), p. 2-33, Figure 36 (Crosswind Component Graph), its printed example: "40 knots wind at 30° angle ... C 35 knots headwind component, D 20 knots crosswind component".
cases.method: Read off the graph to the knot; the engine's 34.6 and 20.0 kt are within 1. The example gives no side; the wind is put 30 degrees right of a heading of 360, so the crosswind is positive.
